task_title: Supplemental Oxygen, Parachutes and Aerobatic Flight
objective: By the end of this lesson you can say when 14 CFR 91.211 requires the crew to use oxygen and when every occupant must have it, recognize the types and signs of hypoxia and why time of useful consciousness is short, and state where aerobatic flight is banned and when parachutes are required.
why: Hypoxia comes on quietly, and its worst early symptom is feeling fine. The AC on high altitude flight calls it a dangerous misconception that pilots can easily spot hypoxia and fix it in time [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]]. The flight review guide lists supplemental oxygen and fitness for flight as cautions to review [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]], and the aerobatic and parachute rules decide what you may do with a friend on board [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]] [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

prereading.what: The oxygen rule itself: the three cabin altitude steps in (a) and the pressurized cabin rules in (b). Short; read every word, and notice "provided with" versus "uses".
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.211

prereading.what: AIM 8-1-2a, Hypoxia: what happens at each cabin altitude, what lowers your tolerance, and the FAA's 10,000 ft day and 5,000 ft night oxygen advice.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-2

prereading.what: The four kinds of hypoxia, the symptom list, treatment and the meaning of time of useful consciousness.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-3 to 17-4

prereading.what: The FAA's deeper look at hypoxia: signs versus symptoms, your hypoxia "signature", pulse oximeter cautions, the DON MASK, DESCEND, LAND drill and the time of useful consciousness table.
prereading.label: AC 61-107B 2-7

prereading.what: Pressurization, decompression, oxygen systems (cannula, masks, pulse-demand), the oxygen preflight and pulse oximeters.
prereading.label: PHAK 7-35 to 7-39

prereading.what: The six places and conditions where aerobatics are banned, and the parachute packing and wearing rules with their exceptions.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.303 and 91.307

prereading.what: AIM 8-1-7, Aerobatic Flight: what G forces do to the body, from red-out to loss of consciousness.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-7

warmup: Think first: You plan a day trip over the mountains in a non-pressurized airplane. The route needs 13,500 ft for about 40 minutes, and a passenger would like to climb to 16,500 ft for a smoother ride. You feel great at altitude and have never used oxygen. What does the rule require for you and for the passenger at each altitude, and why might "I feel great" be the wrong thing to trust?

key_terms.def: The pressure inside the cabin, stated as the altitude above sea level that has that pressure. 91.211 is written in these terms.
The crew the aircraft must have to be flown. 91.211 says when they must use oxygen.
Oxygen and a way to breathe it must be there for the person. The rule does not say they must use it.
Not enough oxygen in the body to keep the brain and other organs working right.
Not enough oxygen reaches the lungs and blood. Altitude causes it by lowering the pressure of the oxygen you breathe.
The blood cannot carry enough oxygen, for example from carbon monoxide, smoking, anemia or blood loss.
Blood is not flowing well enough to the tissues, for example from high G forces, cold or shock.
The cells get oxygen but cannot use it, for example because of alcohol or drugs.
How long you can still take proper corrective action after your oxygen supply is cut off. It gets shorter as altitude rises.
A small clip on the fingertip that shows how saturated your blood is with oxygen, and your heart rate.
Under 91.303, an intentional maneuver with an abrupt change in attitude, an abnormal attitude or abnormal acceleration, not needed for normal flight.
A parachute made under a type certificate or a TSO C-23 series, or certain military personnel parachutes (91.307(e)).

body.p: Every number in 91.211(a) is a cabin pressure altitude, not the altitude printed on a chart or flight plan [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. Cabin altitude is the cabin pressure expressed as the equivalent altitude above sea level [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[11:6|AC 61-107B 1-4d]].

Application: in a non-pressurized airplane the cabin is at the outside pressure, so the cabin pressure altitude is about the airplane's own pressure altitude. A pressurization system keeps the cabin lower than the flight altitude [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. A typical system holds about 8,000 ft at the airplane's maximum designed cruising altitude, where oxygen equipment is not required [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

Pressurized airplanes have instruments for this: a cabin altimeter, a cabin differential pressure gauge (inside versus outside pressure) and a cabin rate-of-climb indicator. Watch the differential gauge so the cabin stays under its maximum allowable differential pressure [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

Why pressure and not oxygen percent? Oxygen stays about 21 percent of the air from the ground to space. Altitude hypoxia comes only from the lower barometric pressure [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a1]]. With less pressure, fewer oxygen molecules are pushed across into your blood [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].

callout.text: At your next flight review, expect this topic. AC 61-98E's regulatory review guide lists Supplemental Oxygen (91.211) and Fitness for Flight (AIM chapter 8, section 1) under Cautions [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]].

check.q: At FL200 a pressurization fault lets the cabin altimeter climb to 13,000 ft, and you have been there 20 minutes. Does 91.211(a) require the crew to use oxygen yet?
check.a: Not yet by rule. At a 13,000 ft cabin pressure altitude the required crew must use it for the time beyond 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]. Application: put it on now, since the cabin may keep climbing.

callout.text: No person may operate a civil aircraft of U.S. registry: (1) above 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft cabin pressure altitude unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses supplemental oxygen for the part of the flight at those altitudes that lasts more than 30 minutes; (2) above 14,000 ft unless the required minimum flight crew is provided with and uses it the entire time at those altitudes; (3) above 15,000 ft unless each occupant is provided with supplemental oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

head: Cabin pressure altitude
Who
What 91.211(a) requires
rows: Nothing. The FAA still encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]].
Above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft
Provided with and uses oxygen for the time at those altitudes beyond 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]
Provided with and uses oxygen the entire time at those altitudes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]]
Provided with oxygen. The crew must still use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]]

body.p: Notice the verbs. The crew must be "provided with and use" oxygen. Above 15,000 ft each occupant must be "provided with" it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. The rule does not make a passenger breathe it. Application: hand it out, show how it works, and encourage its use anyway.

Interpretation: "required minimum flight crew" means the crew the aircraft needs, not everyone on board who holds a certificate. In an airplane flown by one required pilot, that is the pilot flying. A pilot-rated friend riding along is an occupant under (a)(3).

Worked example. You cross a ridge at a cabin altitude of 13,500 ft for 40 minutes. The first 30 minutes need no oxygen by rule; the last 10 do [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]]. Climb to 14,500 ft and you need it from the moment you pass 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]]. Climb to 16,500 ft with passengers and each one must also have oxygen available [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]].

callout.text: 12.5, 14, 15: after half an hour, all the time, everyone gets some. Application: a study aid built from [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

check.q: You cruise at a 13,000 ft cabin altitude for 70 minutes. For how many minutes must the required crew use oxygen?
check.a: 40 minutes: 70 - 30, the part of the flight at those altitudes beyond 30 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]].

callout.text: Pressurized cabin: above FL250, at least a 10-minute supply of oxygen for each occupant, in addition to any oxygen 91.211(a) needs, must be available for a descent forced by loss of pressurization [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(i)]]. Above FL350, one pilot at the controls wears and uses a sealed oxygen mask, unless at or below FL410 there are two pilots at the controls with quick-donning masks that go on with one hand within 5 seconds [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(ii)]]. Above FL350, if one pilot leaves the controls, the other puts on and uses a mask until the first returns [[60:492|14 CFR 91.211(b)(2)]].

body.p: Even pressurized airplanes need oxygen on board, because decompression is always possible [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. Decompression is the system's inability to hold its designed pressure differential, from a system fault or structural damage [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]]. Its main danger is hypoxia, so you need quick, proper use of oxygen equipment and a rapid descent [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

A fast decompression is loud and obvious: noise, fog, flying debris, a wind blast, cold [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]]. A slow one may go unnoticed while hypoxia dulls your mind. The AC warns that slow decompression is as dangerous as, or more dangerous than, a rapid or explosive one [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]].

Pressurized aircraft built to certain part 23 or 25 standards have a cabin altitude warning at 10,000 ft cabin altitude [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]]. Automatic visual and aural warnings are part of pressurized aircraft equipment [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

61.31(g): to act as PIC of a pressurized aircraft whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft MSL, you need logged ground training with an endorsement (it includes hypoxia and how long you stay conscious without oxygen) and flight training with an endorsement (including simulated rapid decompression and emergency descent) [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. Some pilots with earlier documented experience are excepted [[60:215|14 CFR 61.31(g)(3)]].

callout.text: A pressurized cabin is not a reason to skip the oxygen check. The 10-minute supply exists for the descent after pressure is lost [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(i)]], and the time you have to act shrinks fast [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

check.q: What is the 10-minute supply above FL250 for?
check.a: A descent made necessary by loss of cabin pressurization. It is for each occupant, on top of any oxygen 91.211(a) requires [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(i)]].

body.p: Hypoxia is an oxygen deficiency in the body large enough to impair the brain and other organs [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a1]]. The brain is the main concern because it is very sensitive to a lack of oxygen [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. The AC adds that the brain uses about 20 percent of the oxygen you breathe and that judgment and thinking skills drop from the very start [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)]].

head: Type
Where it goes wrong
Examples in the sources
rows: Not enough oxygen gets into the lungs and blood
Lower oxygen pressure at altitude; a blocked airway [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]] [[11:23|AC 61-107B Table 2-4]]
The blood cannot carry enough oxygen
Carbon monoxide, anemia, bleeding, blood donation [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]; smoking and some prescription drugs [[11:23|AC 61-107B Table 2-4]]
Blood is not flowing to the tissues
High G forces, cold, shock, a heart that pumps poorly [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[11:23|AC 61-107B Table 2-4]]
Cells cannot use the oxygen they get

body.p: Two numbers worth remembering. The PHAK says research shows one ounce of alcohol can equal an extra 2,000 ft of physiological altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. The AC says a smoker's physiological altitude at sea level is about 7,000 ft, and 20,000 ft for a nonsmoker is like 22,000 ft for a smoker [[11:24|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(b)]].

Carbon monoxide is colorless, odorless and tasteless. Most light airplane heaters pass air over the exhaust manifold, so a crack can feed it into the cabin. If you smell exhaust or get a headache, drowsiness or dizziness with the heater on, shut the heater off and open the air vents [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

callout.text: Air, blood, flow, cells: hypoxic, hypemic, stagnant, histotoxic. Application: a study aid built from [[11:23|AC 61-107B Table 2-4]].

check.q: Why can a pilot with a cracked exhaust become hypoxic at 4,500 ft?
check.a: Carbon monoxide keeps the blood from carrying oxygen, which is hypemic hypoxia [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]], so altitude is not needed [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

chunks.title: Symptoms: what happens as the cabin climbs

head: Cabin pressure altitude
What the AIM says
rows: Other significant effects usually do not occur in a normal healthy pilot [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a2]]

Judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and calculations are impaired; headache, drowsiness, dizziness, and either euphoria or belligerence. Performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a2]]
Tunnel vision and blue fingernails and lips (cyanosis) [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a3]]
The ability to take corrective and protective action is lost in 20 to 30 minutes [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a3]]

body.p: The AC adds a caution to the "below 12,000 ft" line: there is no guarantee it always holds, and impairment is a continuum with no exact altitude where it starts or stops [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].

bullets: PHAK symptom list: cyanosis, headache, slower reactions, impaired judgment, euphoria, visual impairment, drowsiness, light-headedness or dizziness, tingling in fingers and toes, numbness [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

Order: early symptoms can include euphoria and a carefree feeling. Then hands and feet respond less well and flying gets less coordinated. As it worsens, vision narrows and the instruments become hard to read [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

Signs (what an observer can see, such as rapid breathing, cyanosis, poor coordination, poor judgment) differ from symptoms (what you feel, such as air hunger, headache, tingling, euphoria) [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].

The AC calls euphoria, a false sense of well-being, probably the most dangerous symptom, and visual impairment probably the least reliable, because it comes on too slowly to notice [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].

body.p: Your own pattern repeats. The AIM says symptoms do not vary in an individual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a5]]. The AC explains that people differ, but the order and strength of your own symptoms usually stay the same over the years, your hypoxia "signature" [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]]. An altitude chamber flight is the way to learn it; the FAA offers this training at CAMI [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a5]] [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-8]].

A look-alike: hyperventilation, breathing too fast and deep, causes light-headedness, tingling and drowsiness too, and it can happen together with hypoxia [[34:183|AIM 8-1-3]]. Slowing your breathing or talking aloud helps it [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

check.q: At a 15,500 ft cabin altitude you feel unusually cheerful and a passenger says your lips look blue. What is happening?
check.a: Euphoria and cyanosis are hypoxia symptoms [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], and cyanosis appears above 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a3]]. Get on oxygen and descend [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].

body.p: Time of useful consciousness (TUC) is the time from losing your oxygen supply until you can no longer take proper corrective and protective action [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]]. The PHAK calls it the most time you have to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions without supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. It falls quickly as altitude rises above 10,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

callout.text: TUC does not mean the start of unconsciousness. Impaired performance may be immediate, so use 100 percent oxygen at once [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]].

body.p: The table shows averages with wide differences between people. The AC says the safest approach is to treat the lower TUC value as the limit [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Rapid loss of pressurization cuts TUC sharply: as a general rule by 50 percent between 25,000 and 43,000 ft [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

bullets: TUC also gets shorter with a faster climb, physical activity (10 deep knee bends at 25,000 ft without a mask cut it by half), fatigue, low blood sugar, alcohol, some medications, smoking, poor fitness and illness [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)(b)]].
Impairment grows with altitude, with harder and more complex tasks, and with new tasks compared to practiced ones [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)(b)]].

body.p: The AIM puts the 18,000 ft and 20,000 ft points this way: corrective action is lost in 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 ft and in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft, followed soon by unconsciousness [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a3]].

check.q: In AC 61-107B Figure 2-3, what is the TUC at 25,000 ft, and what is it after a rapid decompression?
check.a: 3 to 5 minutes normally, and 1.5 to 2.5 minutes following rapid decompression [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]].

chunks.title: Oxygen equipment, preflight and pulse oximeters

body.p: Airplanes without a fixed oxygen system need portable equipment readily accessible in flight: container, regulator, mask outlet and pressure gauge. Oxygen is usually stored at 1,800 to 2,200 psi. Cylinder pressure drops when the cylinder gets cold, so a lower reading may be temperature rather than a leak. Use aviator's breathing oxygen that meets SAE AS8010 [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]]. Fasten the container securely before flight [[11:38|AC 61-107B 2-9b]].

bullets: Cannula: tubing under the nose. More comfortable than a mask, but may not supply oxygen as reliably at higher altitudes. The PHAK says installed systems certified above 18,000 ft must have masks instead. If it has a green flow detector, check it as part of your scan [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
Continuous flow: common for passengers; the mask has a reservoir bag that stores oxygen while you exhale [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
Diluter demand: oxygen flows only when you inhale, and a tight-sealing mask is safe up to 40,000 ft. Beards and mustaches can break the seal [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
Pressure demand: like diluter demand, but pushes oxygen under pressure at cabin altitudes above 34,000 ft [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].
Electrical pulse demand: gives a pulse of oxygen at the start of each breath and can cut oxygen use by 50 to 85 percent compared with continuous flow [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

body.p: Preflight: inspect and test all oxygen equipment before each flight, with clean hands. Look over the mask and tubing for tears, cracks or wear; check the regulator valves and levers, the quantity, the gauges, flow indicators and connections; put the mask on and test the system. After any use, make sure every valve is shut off [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b(3)]]. Confirm the oxygen is readily accessible [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

callout.text: Oxygen feeds fire. Materials that barely burn in normal air can burn in oxygen, oils and greases can ignite, and smoking during any oxygen use is prohibited [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

body.p: A pulse oximeter estimates blood oxygen saturation from a light beam through the fingertip, within about one percent of a direct blood measurement. The PHAK calls it very useful in non-pressurized airplanes above 12,500 ft, so crew and passengers can judge their real need for oxygen [[1:199|PHAK 7-39]].

check.q: You land and are done with the oxygen. What must you verify?
check.a: That all components and valves are shut off [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]] [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b(3)]].

chunks.title: Risk: "I feel fine, so I don't need oxygen"

callout.text: The AC calls it a common misconception that hypoxia symptoms are easy to recognize in time to act. It calls that idea misleading and dangerous [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].

body.p: Why feeling fine proves nothing: hypoxia effects are hard to recognize, especially when they come on slowly [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a5]]. Hypoxia can give you a false sense of security [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Onset is usually insidious, and being busy with flying duties can let it go past the point of self-help [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].
Things that lower the altitude where hypoxia hits you [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a4]]:

bullets: Carbon monoxide from smoking or exhaust, anemia and some medications reduce how much oxygen the blood can carry.
Small amounts of alcohol and low doses of drugs such as antihistamines, tranquilizers, sedatives and pain relievers make the brain more susceptible.
Extreme heat or cold, fever and anxiety raise the body's oxygen demand.

body.p: At night, especially when tired, effects can show up as low as 5,000 ft [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. Vision also degrades with altitude, and smoking makes that worse [[11:35|AC 61-107B 2-7f]].

head: Legal minimum (91.211(a))
FAA recommendation
rows: Crew uses oxygen after 30 minutes above 12,500 ft, and all the time above 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]

callout.text: Do not let the pulse oximeter be your only alarm. The FAA cautions that waiting for the reading to fall can mean you are already impaired, and the finger reading may not show what reaches the brain [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(f), (g)]].

If you suspect hypoxia: DON MASK within 5 seconds, check the flow and breathe 100 percent oxygen; DESCEND, preferably below 10,000 ft; LAND as soon as possible where medical help is available [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]]. Recovery after 100 percent oxygen usually comes within seconds [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(f), (g)]].

check.q: Name three things besides altitude that the AIM says make you more susceptible to hypoxia.
check.a: Any three of: carbon monoxide (smoking or exhaust), anemia, certain medications, small amounts of alcohol, antihistamines or sedatives, extreme heat or cold, fever, anxiety [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a4]].

callout.text: Aerobatic flight means an intentional maneuver with an abrupt change in attitude, an abnormal attitude or abnormal acceleration, not necessary for normal flight [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

head: No aerobatics
Notes
rows: (a) Over any congested area of a city, town or settlement
The rule does not define "congested" [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]
(b) Over an open air assembly of persons
(c) Within the lateral boundaries of the surface areas of Class B, C, D or E airspace designated for an airport
The rule says "lateral boundaries" and names no altitude [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. A Class E surface area is charted with a magenta dashed line [[2:17|Chart Users' Guide p 17]]
(d) Within 4 NM of the center line of any Federal airway

A Federal airway itself extends 4 NM each side of its centerline, with a floor of 1,200 ft AGL unless otherwise specified [[23:23|IFH 1-4]]. The 91.303 text gives no altitude limit for this band [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]
(f) When flight visibility is less than 3 SM

body.p: Sectionals mark aerobatic practice areas with the symbol above [[2:46|Chart Users' Guide p 46]]. The legend shows the symbol only; it does not say the area changes any part of 91.303.

G forces: a rapid push-over shoves blood toward the head and can cause headache, "red-out" and even unconsciousness. A rapid pull-up or a steep turn drains blood from the head: narrowing vision, gray-out, black-out, then unconsciousness. Even a brief blackout can lead to a control input that breaks the airplane or hits something [[34:187|AIM 8-1-7]]. This is the stagnant hypoxia the PHAK links to excessive G [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Tolerance improves with practice and depends on the person, physical condition and recent exposure. Consult an Aviation Medical Examiner before aerobatic training [[34:188|AIM 8-1-7e]].

Aerobatic training is not upset training. In aerobatics you know the maneuver is coming, so there is no startle; its goal is precise maneuvering. Upset prevention and recovery training (UPRT) aims at recovering from unplanned upsets [[24:110|AFH 5-5]].

check.q: You plan a loop over open country, 6 NM from any airway, outside all surface areas, bottoming out at 1,800 ft AGL with 5 SM visibility. Does 91.303 allow it?
check.a: Yes. None of the six limits applies: not below 1,500 ft, visibility not under 3 SM, not within 4 NM of an airway, not in a surface area, not over a congested area or crowd [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. If a non-crewmember is aboard, 91.307 parachute rules may also apply [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

callout.text: Unless each occupant is wearing an approved parachute, no pilot carrying any person other than a crewmember may make an intentional maneuver that exceeds a bank of 60 degrees or a nose-up or nose-down attitude of 30 degrees relative to the horizon [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

body.p: A crewmember is a person assigned to perform duty in an aircraft during flight time [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]]. So the rule bites when you carry a passenger. "Each occupant" includes you, the pilot [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

Exceptions in 91.307(d): flight tests for a pilot certificate or rating, and spins and other maneuvers required by the regulations for any certificate or rating when given by a CFI or by an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]].

head: Parachute carried for emergency use
Must be packed by a certificated, appropriately rated rigger within
rows: Canopy, shrouds and harness all nylon, rayon or similar synthetic
Any part silk, pongee or other natural fiber

body.p: It must also be an approved type: made under a type certificate or a TSO C-23 series, or certain military personnel parachutes [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(e)]]. Jumping is a different matter: except in an emergency, a parachute operation from an aircraft must follow part 105 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(b)]].

callout.text: Before spin training, the AFH says to review the AFM/POH limitations and placards, weight and balance, the entry and recovery procedures, and the current part 91 parachute requirements [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

The 60 and 30 degree limits apply to intentional maneuvers with a passenger aboard and no parachutes [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. Application: a steep "show-off" turn or a sharp pull-up for a friend counts.

check.q: A CFI gives a student the spin training required for the student's flight instructor certificate. Neither wears a parachute. Does 91.307 allow it?
check.a: Yes. Spins required by the regulations for a certificate, given by a CFI, are excepted from 91.307(c) [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]].

bullets: Reading 91.211 off the chart altitude in a pressurized airplane. Fix: use cabin pressure altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].
Giving yourself 30 minutes above 14,000 ft. Fix: the 30 minutes applies only up to 14,000 ft; above it the crew uses oxygen the whole time [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]].
Thinking passengers must wear oxygen above 15,000 ft. Fix: they must be provided with it; the crew must use it [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].
Treating the legal minimum as the safe level. Fix: the FAA encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]].

Trusting "I feel fine" or the oximeter alone. Fix: hypoxia is insidious and euphoria is its most dangerous symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]]; the oximeter is not a sole indicator [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(f), (g)]].
Skipping the oxygen preflight. Fix: inspect, don the mask and test the system before each flight [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b(3)]].
Doing aerobatics above a Class D airport's ceiling. Fix: 91.303(c) uses the surface area's lateral boundaries [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].
Showing a passenger a 70 degree bank. Fix: no more than 60 degrees bank or 30 degrees pitch unless everyone wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

check.q: Above which cabin altitude does the 30-minute allowance stop applying to the crew?
check.a: Above 14,000 ft, where the crew must use oxygen the entire time [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]].

scenario.title: The ski town trip
scenario.setup: You fly a non-pressurized, turbocharged single-engine airplane with three passengers to a mountain ski town on a winter morning. The plan is 14,500 ft for about 70 minutes over the high terrain. You carry a portable oxygen bottle with four cannulas and a pulse oximeter. One passenger has a fever and is nervous about flying. At the destination, a friend offers you an aerobatic ride in his two-seat aerobatic airplane.

questions.q: At 14,500 ft for 70 minutes, what does 91.211 require for you and for the passengers?
questions.a: You, the required crew, must use oxygen the entire time above 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]]. Nothing is required for the passengers below 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]], though the FAA encourages oxygen above 10,000 ft by day [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]].

questions.q: Over the highest terrain the oxygen bottle fails. What does AC 61-107B advise, and what makes it hard here?
questions.a: If supplemental oxygen is not available, start an emergency descent to below 10,000 ft MSL, and land as soon as possible if symptoms persist [[11:23|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(a)]]. Application: over high terrain you may not be able to get that low, so head toward lower terrain and descend as far as terrain clearance allows; plan that escape route before you go.

questions.q: Why should you watch the passenger with a fever more closely?
questions.a: Fever and anxiety increase the body's oxygen demand and so its susceptibility to hypoxia [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a4]].

questions.q: Halfway there you feel sharp and decide you could do without the cannula. What is wrong with that reasoning?
questions.a: Hypoxia effects are hard to recognize, especially when gradual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a5]], euphoria is probably the most dangerous symptom [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]], and above 14,000 ft the rule requires oxygen anyway [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]].

questions.q: Your friend suggests aerobatics over the frozen lake by the town, where people are skating, at 2,000 ft AGL. Problem?
questions.a: Yes. No aerobatics over an open air assembly of persons, or over a congested area of a town [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. Move away from people, the town, any airport surface area and any airway's 4 NM band, and stay at or above 1,500 ft with at least 3 SM visibility [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

questions.q: You will ride along as a passenger. What do you both need, and how fresh must the parachutes be?
questions.a: Maneuvers beyond 60 degrees bank or 30 degrees pitch with a non-crewmember aboard need each occupant to wear an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. Nylon parachutes must have been packed by a certificated rigger within 180 days, and any with natural fiber within 60 days [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]].

skills.do: Given a flight (route altitudes and times, pressurized or not, day or night, who is aboard), say when the required crew must use oxygen, when each occupant must be provided with it, what the FAA recommends beyond the rule, and what you would do if hypoxia were suspected.
skills.practice: Take two of your own routes, one over high terrain. For each leg write the cabin altitude, the minutes there, and which 91.211(a) step applies [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. Add the 10,000 ft day and 5,000 ft night advice [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]]. Then preflight a portable oxygen system with a CFI using the PHAK and AC checklist items [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b(3)]], and say the DON MASK, DESCEND, LAND drill aloud [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].

quiz.q: In a pressurized airplane, which instrument checks the cabin pressure altitude?
options: The airplane's main altimeter
The cabin rate-of-climb indicator
The cabin altimeter
The manifold pressure gauge
quiz.why: A cabin altimeter is provided as a check on the system's performance; the rate-of-climb indicator shows the cabin's rate of climb or descent [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

options: The airplane's height above the ground
The cabin pressure expressed as the equivalent altitude above sea level
The altitude on the flight plan
The difference between cabin and outside pressure
quiz.why: Cabin altitude is cabin pressure in terms of equivalent altitude above sea level [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]] [[11:6|AC 61-107B 1-4d]]. The pressure difference is the differential pressure [[1:195|PHAK 7-35]].

quiz.q: Above FL350 in a pressurized aircraft, what does 91.211(b) require of the pilots?
options: Every occupant wears a mask
Nothing beyond the 10-minute supply
Oxygen only if the cabin exceeds 15,000 ft
One pilot at the controls wears and uses a sealed mask, with an exception for two pilots with quick-donning masks at or below FL410

quiz.q: Alcohol keeps the body's cells from using the oxygen they receive. What type of hypoxia is that?
options: Hypoxic
Hypemic
Stagnant
Histotoxic
quiz.why: Histotoxic hypoxia is the cells' inability to use oxygen, caused by alcohol and other drugs [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[11:23|AC 61-107B Table 2-4]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, night vision starts to deteriorate at a cabin pressure altitude as low as:
quiz.why: A deterioration in night vision occurs at a cabin pressure altitude as low as 5,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a2]].

quiz.q: Which best describes time of useful consciousness?
options: The time until you pass out
The time it takes to recover after using oxygen
The time from losing your oxygen supply until you can no longer take proper corrective action
The legal time allowed above 12,500 ft
quiz.why: TUC runs until you are no longer capable of taking proper corrective and protective action, and it does not mean the onset of unconsciousness [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]].

quiz.q: Which hypoxia symptom does AC 61-107B call probably the most dangerous?
options: Headache
Nausea
Euphoria, a false sense of well-being
Hot and cold flashes
quiz.why: Of all the symptoms, euphoria is probably the most dangerous [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].

quiz.q: Under 91.303, no aerobatic flight when flight visibility is less than:
options: 1 SM
3 SM
5 SM
10 SM
quiz.why: No aerobatic flight when flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

quiz.q: A parachute with an all-nylon canopy, shrouds and harness may be carried for emergency use if a certificated rigger packed it within the preceding:
options: 60 days
90 days
120 days
180 days
quiz.why: Synthetic fiber parachutes: within the preceding 180 days [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You fly a single-pilot airplane as PIC with a private pilot friend in the right seat as a passenger. You cruise at a 14,500 ft cabin altitude for 40 minutes. What does 91.211 require?
options: Both of you must use oxygen the whole time
Both of you must use it after 30 minutes
You must use oxygen the whole time above 14,000 ft; nothing is required for your friend
Only your friend must be provided with oxygen
final_quiz.why: The required minimum flight crew uses oxygen the entire time above 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]]. Your friend is not required crew (interpretation), and occupants need oxygen provided only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: You buy a pressurized single whose service ceiling is 25,000 ft MSL and whose maximum operating altitude is also 25,000 ft. Do you need the 61.31(g) high-altitude endorsements to act as PIC?
options: No; 61.31(g) applies when the lower of the two is above 25,000 ft MSL
Yes; every pressurized airplane needs them
Yes, but only the ground training
Only if you fly above FL180
final_quiz.why: 61.31(g) defines a pressurized aircraft for this rule as one with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 ft MSL [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]]. Application: the training is still a good idea.

final_quiz.q: At a 12,000 ft cabin altitude in daylight, your passenger becomes argumentative and can't add up the fuel figures. What is the most likely cause and the best response?
options: Motion sickness; open the vents
Fatigue; let her nap
Hypoxia; give her oxygen and descend
Hyperventilation; ignore it, it always passes
final_quiz.why: From 12,000 to 15,000 ft calculations are impaired and belligerence can occur [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a2]]. Treatment is oxygen and a lower altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].

final_quiz.q: You brief a possible oxygen loss at 28,000 ft. AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 gives 2.5 to 3 minutes of TUC there. What should you plan on?
options: 3 minutes, the average
2.5 minutes, because the AC says to treat the lower value as limiting, and impairment may start at once
About 30 minutes, as at lower altitudes
Until the pulse oximeter alarms
final_quiz.why: TUCs are averages with wide individual variation; the safest approach is to assume the lower value is limiting [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Impaired performance may be immediate [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Your passenger smokes heavily. What does AC 61-107B say about her?
options: Smoking only matters above 25,000 ft
Her physiological altitude is higher than the actual altitude, so set or fly a lower cabin altitude
She will notice hypoxia sooner and is safer
Smoking affects only night vision
final_quiz.why: Smokers' physiological altitudes are much higher than actual; at sea level about 7,000 ft. A lower cabin altitude should be set [[11:24|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(b)]].

final_quiz.q: You want to fly aerobatics 12 NM from the nearest airport in Class E airspace with a 700 ft AGL floor, at 3,500 ft AGL, 6 NM from any airway, over open country, 8 SM visibility. Legal under 91.303?
options: No, aerobatics are banned in all Class E airspace
Yes; only Class E surface areas designated for an airport are excluded, and the other limits are met
No, you must be above 5,000 ft AGL
Only with ATC approval
final_quiz.why: 91.303(c) bans aerobatics within the lateral boundaries of surface areas of Class B, C, D or E designated for an airport, not all Class E. The other limits are met [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

final_quiz.q: A Class D airport's airspace tops out at 2,500 ft AGL. You plan aerobatics at 4,000 ft AGL directly above the field. Legal under 91.303?
options: Yes, you are above the Class D ceiling
Yes, if you talk to the tower
No, the rule bans aerobatics within the lateral boundaries of the surface area, with no altitude limit
No, only because you are below 5,000 ft AGL
final_quiz.why: 91.303(c) uses the surface area's lateral boundaries and names no altitude [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]].

final_quiz.q: With a non-crewmember passenger aboard and no parachutes, which intentional maneuver is NOT allowed?
options: A 45 degree steep turn
A 25 degree nose-up climb
A 35 degree nose-down attitude
A 55 degree bank turn
final_quiz.why: Without approved parachutes on each occupant, you may not exceed 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose-up or nose-down [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]].

final_quiz.q: A vintage parachute with a silk canopy was packed by a certificated rigger 90 days ago. May you carry it for emergency use?
options: Yes, the limit is 180 days
No, any natural fiber parachute must have been packed within the preceding 60 days
Yes, if it is an approved type
Yes, if no one plans to use it
final_quiz.why: Silk, pongee or other natural fiber: packed within the preceding 60 days [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]].

final_quiz.q: A friend wants to make a skydive from your airplane. What does 91.307 say?
options: Allowed if he wears an approved parachute
Allowed below 1,500 ft AGL only
Except in an emergency, a parachute operation must be done under part 105
Banned for all civil aircraft
final_quiz.why: Except in an emergency, no PIC may allow and no person may conduct a parachute operation except under part 105 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(b)]].

final_quiz.q: In a pressurized single at FL220 the cabin altitude creeps up slowly, with no noise or fog. How does AC 61-107B rate this compared with a loud, rapid decompression?
options: Less dangerous, since there is more time
Harmless unless the cabin passes 18,000 ft
Dangerous only at night
As dangerous or more dangerous, because it may go unnoticed while hypoxia dulls your judgment
final_quiz.why: Slow decompression is as dangerous as or more dangerous than rapid decompression; a rapid one commands attention, a slow one may go unnoticed [[11:28|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)]].

final_quiz.q: A pilot says, "I'll know I'm hypoxic when my vision goes." What does AC 61-107B say about that symptom?
options: Vision loss is the first and most reliable sign
Vision is never affected by hypoxia
Visual impairment is probably the least reliable symptom, because the visual field changes too slowly to notice
Vision changes only above 25,000 ft
final_quiz.why: Of the listed symptoms, visual impairment is probably the least reliable; the visual field is affected at such a slow rate it could go unnoticed [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]].

final_quiz.q: Before aerobatic training, what does the AIM recommend about your health?
options: Nothing; G tolerance is the same for everyone
Consult an Aviation Medical Examiner, and know poor physical condition lowers G tolerance
Get a first-class medical
Take a decongestant before each flight
final_quiz.why: Consult an AME before aerobatic training and be aware that poor physical condition can reduce tolerance to G forces [[34:188|AIM 8-1-7e]].

takeaways: Above 12,500 ft: crew uses oxygen after 30 minutes. Above 14,000 ft: crew uses it the whole time. Above 15,000 ft: everyone is provided with it.
Pressurized above FL250: a 10-minute supply for each occupant for the descent.
Four types of hypoxia: hypoxic, hypemic, stagnant, histotoxic. Feeling fine, even euphoric, is a symptom, not a clearance.
TUC is short and is not the time until you pass out; treat the lower table value as your limit.
No aerobatics over towns or crowds, in airport surface areas, within 4 NM of an airway centerline, below 1,500 ft AGL, or under 3 SM visibility.
With a passenger aboard, beyond 60 degrees bank or 30 degrees pitch everyone wears an approved parachute: synthetic packed within 180 days, natural fiber within 60.
cfi_notes: PHAK Figure 17-1 lists "30 minutes or more" of TUC at 20,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. The AIM says corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a3]], and AC 61-107B Figure 2-3 gives 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 ft and 10 minutes at 22,000 ft [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]]. Teach the AIM; this lesson shows the AC table instead of the PHAK one.

On rapid decompression, the PHAK says effective performance time is reduced "by one-third to one-fourth its normal time" [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]], while AC 61-107B says TUC is reduced by 50 percent between 25,000 and 43,000 ft as a general rule [[11:29|AC 61-107B Figure 2-3]] and by at least 50 percent [[11:30|AC 61-107B 2-7e(3)(b)]]. The wording differs; the lesson teaches the AC table numbers and the shared point that TUC drops sharply.

The PHAK calls carbon monoxide poisoning the most common form of hypemic hypoxia [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]; AC 61-107B calls smoking the most common cause, with exhaust CO also a consideration [[11:23|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(b)]]. Smoking adds carbon monoxide, so they overlap; this lesson avoids a "most common" question.

The AIM says hypoxia symptoms do not vary in an individual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a5]]; the PHAK says they can be different for each individual [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. AC 61-107B reconciles them: people differ, but each person's order and intensity usually stay constant [[11:25|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(e)]]. Use that to sell altitude chamber training.

AIM 8-1-3c says to set 100 percent oxygen and check the system before working on breathing rate [[34:183|AIM 8-1-3]]. AC 61-107B lists 100 percent oxygen, slower breathing, checking equipment, then descent, to be done together [[11:22|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)]]. Teach both as "oxygen first, then the rest at once" (interpretation) rather than a strict order.

Interpretation: "required minimum flight crew" in 91.211(a) is not defined there [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. In a single-pilot airplane it is normally the pilot flying; a two-pilot crew requirement comes from the aircraft's documents, which these sources do not show.

Interpretation: 91.307(c) applies when "carrying any person (other than a crewmember)" [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. The sources do not say when a student or instructor counts as a crewmember under 1.1 [[60:4|14 CFR 1.1]]. The (d) exceptions cover only required certificate or rating maneuvers by a CFI or ATP; for spins in a flight review or UPRT, check FAA legal interpretations before flying without parachutes.

AC 61-98E's flight review guide lists 91.211 and AIM 8-1 but not 91.303 or 91.307 [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]]. Ask pilots who fly with friends about the parachute limits anyway; the 60 and 30 degree limits are easy to bust in a steep turn demo.
Teaching tip: have the pilot bring their own oxygen system and oximeter, run the AC preflight items [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b(3)]], and time a 5 second mask don [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].
gaps: How to count the 30 minutes in 91.211(a)(1) (one continuous period or total time) is not spelled out in these sources.
No source here gives a target pulse oximeter saturation number; the AC only cautions against relying on the oximeter alone. Use the oxygen system maker's guidance and a CFI or AME.

Flow settings, duration and cannula altitude limits for a specific portable system come from its manufacturer and the POH/AFM supplement. The rule behind the PHAK's "masks above 18,000 ft" statement for installed systems is not in these sources.
91.303 does not define "congested area" or "open air assembly of persons", and the Chart Users' Guide does not say what an aerobatic practice area allows.
Part 105 (parachute operations) and FAA legal interpretations of 91.307 are not covered in these sources.

activities.title: Read the pressurization gauge
activities.intro: Drag each label to its pin on the cabin/differential pressure indicator.
activities.why: PHAK Figure 7-42 labels the outer scale as the cabin pressure altitude indicator in thousands of feet, the inner scale as cabin differential pressure in psi, and the red mark as the maximum cabin differential pressure limit [[1:196|PHAK 7-36]].

activities.title: What does 91.211(a) require?
activities.intro: Non-pressurized airplane, one required pilot, two passengers. Tap each case, then tap what the rule requires.
buckets: Pilot uses oxygen for the time beyond 30 minutes
Pilot uses oxygen the whole time
Pilot uses oxygen the whole time, and each passenger must be provided with it
activities.why: (a)(1) covers above 12,500 up to and including 14,000 ft, beyond 30 minutes; (a)(2) above 14,000 ft, the entire time; (a)(3) above 15,000 ft, each occupant provided with oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]]. 12,500 ft is not above 12,500, and 15,000 ft is not above 15,000.

activities.title: True or false: the oxygen rules
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: 91.211's altitude limits are measured as cabin pressure altitude.
cards.why: True. Each step in (a) is a cabin pressure altitude [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

cards.s: 91.211(a) applies to civil aircraft of U.S. registry.
cards.why: True. Its opening words are "civil aircraft of U.S. registry" [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)]].

cards.s: A typical pressurization system holds the cabin near 8,000 ft at the airplane's maximum designed cruising altitude.
Above 14,000 ft cabin altitude, the required crew may fly 30 minutes before using oxygen.
cards.why: False. Above 14,000 ft the crew uses oxygen the entire time [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]].

cards.s: Above FL250 in a pressurized airplane, at least a 10-minute oxygen supply per occupant is needed on top of any 91.211(a) oxygen.
Pressurized aircraft built to certain part 23 or 25 standards warn the crew when the cabin altitude reaches 10,000 ft.
cards.why: True. Such aircraft have cabin altitude warning systems that activate at 10,000 ft cabin altitude [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9c]].

activities.title: What the AIM says happens at each altitude
activities.intro: Tap a cabin altitude, then the effect the AIM gives for it.

pairs.r: Other significant effects usually absent in a healthy pilot
Judgment, memory and calculations impaired; euphoria or belligerence
Performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes

activities.title: How hypoxia gets worse
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put these in the order they usually appear as hypoxia deepens, then tap Check.
steps: Hands and feet respond less well; flying gets less coordinated
Field of vision narrows; instruments get hard to read
Ability to take corrective action is lost, soon followed by unconsciousness
activities.why: The PHAK gives the first three in this order [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; the AIM describes the loss of corrective action followed by unconsciousness [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2a3]].

activities.title: Night over the mountains, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You fly a non-pressurized single at night over a mountain range with two passengers. You carry a portable pulse-demand oxygen system with cannulas and a pulse oximeter. The route needs 13,500 ft for about 50 minutes.

steps.s: Planning. When will you start using oxygen?
options: After 30 minutes at 13,500 ft, the legal minimum
Early in the climb; the FAA encourages oxygen above 5,000 ft at night, and the rule requires it after 30 minutes above 12,500 ft
Only if you start to feel symptoms
Only above 15,000 ft
steps.why: Oxygen above 5,000 ft at night is the FAA recommendation [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]]; the rule requires crew oxygen beyond 30 minutes above 12,500 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(1)]].

steps.s: Preflight. One cannula's tubing has a small crack near its connector. What do you do?
options: Use it; a small crack loses little oxygen
Tape it and skip the system test
Give it to the passenger who will need it least
Replace that cannula, then don one and test the system before flight
steps.why: The preflight includes looking at the mask and tubing for tears, cracks or deterioration, then donning the mask and testing the system [[11:39|AC 61-107B 2-9b(3)]].

steps.s: Cruise. A passenger is giggling, says her fingers tingle, and her lips look bluish. What do you do?
options: Laugh along; she is just happy
Check her cannula and flow, make sure she breathes oxygen, and descend if you can do so safely
Climb to smoother air
Open the vents and wait
steps.why: Euphoria, tingling and cyanosis are hypoxia symptoms [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Treatment is oxygen and a lower altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], checking flow [[11:27|AC 61-107B Table 2-6]].

steps.s: ATC offers 15,500 ft to clear terrain-induced turbulence. What must be true if you accept?
options: Nothing changes
Only the passengers need oxygen
You use oxygen the whole time above 14,000 ft, and each passenger must be provided with it
You need a pressurized airplane
steps.why: Crew: entire time above 14,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(2)]]. Occupants: provided with oxygen above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(a)(3)]].

steps.s: Descent. The oximeter reads normal at 8,000 ft. Do you take off the cannula now?
options: Yes, the oximeter says you are fine
Keep using it down to about 5,000 ft at night; the oximeter is not a sole indicator
Yes, below 12,500 ft oxygen does nothing
Turn the flow up to 100 percent
steps.why: The FAA recommends oxygen above 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2a6]], and cautions against relying on the oximeter alone [[11:26|AC 61-107B 2-7d(2)(f), (g)]].

activities.title: Work the numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A pressurized single will cruise at FL260 with one pilot and five passengers. What is the least total oxygen supply 91.211(b)(1)(i) requires, in person-minutes?
items.why: At least a 10-minute supply for each occupant [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211(b)(1)(i)]]: 6 occupants x 10 minutes = 60 person-minutes, on top of any 91.211(a) oxygen.

items.q: AC 61-107B gives 3 to 5 minutes of TUC at 25,000 ft and says 10 deep knee bends there without a mask cut TUC by 50 percent. What is the shortest TUC after the knee bends, in seconds?
Your all-nylon parachute was packed by a certificated rigger 150 days ago. About how many more days may it be carried for emergency use?
You are 2.7 NM from a Victor airway centerline. How much farther (NM) must you move away to be outside the 91.303(d) band?
